questions.prompt: How is an op-amp's input offset voltage \(V_{os}\) modeled?
options: As a resistor in series with the output
As a small DC voltage source in series with one input of an otherwise offset-free op-amp
As a small AC noise source at the output
As a current source between the two inputs
questions.explanation:
Reader Fig. 18.1: mismatches inside the op-amp act like a DC voltage at the input. Because its sign is random from part to part, it can be drawn at either input. It shifts the input-output transfer curve sideways (Fig. 18.2).
• Noise is random AC; offset is a DC value fixed for a given part.

questions.prompt: An op-amp with \(A_0=10^5\) and \(V_{os}=1\ \mathrm{mV}\) is used OPEN LOOP with both inputs grounded, on \(\pm12\ \mathrm{V}\) supplies. What is the output?
options: Saturated at one rail (about \(\pm12\ \mathrm{V}\)); the ideal 100 V is impossible
0 V, since the inputs are grounded
100 mV
1 mV
questions.explanation:
\(A_0V_{os}=10^5\times1\ \mathrm{mV}=100\ \mathrm{V}\), far beyond the supplies, so the output rails out (reader Sec. 18.2.1). Which rail depends on the sign of \(V_{os}\), which differs part to part.
That's why op-amps are almost always used with negative feedback.

questions.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier has \(R_2/R_1=10\) (gain 11) and an op-amp with \(V_{os}=2\ \mathrm{mV}\). With the input grounded, what is the output offset voltage, in mV?
questions.explanation: \(V_{os}\) sits in series with the \(+\) input, exactly where the signal goes, so it is amplified by the non-inverting gain: \(V_o=V_{os}(1+R_2/R_1)=2\ \mathrm{mV}\times11=22\ \mathrm{mV}\).

questions.prompt: An INVERTING amplifier has \(R_2/R_1=10\) (signal gain \(-10\)) and an op-amp with \(V_{os}=2\ \mathrm{mV}\). With the signal input grounded, what is the magnitude of the output offset, in mV?
questions.explanation:
With \(v_{in}=0\), the inverting amplifier's input resistor \(R_1\) goes to ground, so the circuit is identical to a non-inverting amplifier for \(V_{os}\): the offset sees the 'noise gain' \(1+R_2/R_1=11\). \(|V_o|=11\times2\ \mathrm{mV}=22\ \mathrm{mV}\), not 20 mV.
Common mistake: multiplying by the signal gain 10.

questions.prompt: A gain-100 non-inverting amplifier must have an output offset below 50 mV. What is the largest acceptable \(|V_{os}|\), in mV?
questions.explanation: \(|V_{o}|=100|V_{os}|\le50\ \mathrm{mV}\Rightarrow|V_{os}|\le0.5\ \mathrm{mV}\). High-gain DC amplifiers need low-offset (or trimmed) op-amps.

questions.prompt: A datasheet lists an offset voltage of 2 mV. How should you interpret it for a batch of parts?
options: Every part has exactly \(+2\ \mathrm{mV}\)
The offset changes sign every cycle like an AC signal
It's the output offset in any circuit
Each part has its own fixed offset with random sign; 2 mV describes the statistical spread (the reader notes it is usually the standard deviation), so some parts exceed it
questions.explanation: Offset comes from random mismatch (reader Sec. 18.2.1), so it varies from part to part, with either sign. For a robust design use the worst-case or several-σ value, and remember the circuit multiplies it by the noise gain.

questions.prompt: An inverting amplifier with gain \(-1\) (\(R_2=R_1\)) uses an op-amp with \(V_{os}=3\ \mathrm{mV}\). What is the output offset magnitude?
options: 3 mV (gain magnitude 1)
0 V, because the gain is \(-1\) and the offset cancels
6 mV (offset gain \(1+R_2/R_1=2\))
1.5 mV
questions.explanation: The offset is amplified by \(1+R_2/R_1=2\), the gain from the \(+\) input, whatever the signal gain is. A '\(-1\)' stage still doubles the offset.

questions.prompt: An inverting amplifier has \(R_2/R_1=50\), a DC input \(v_{in}=+10\ \mathrm{mV}\), and \(V_{os}=+1\ \mathrm{mV}\) modeled in series with the \(+\) input (so \(V^+=+1\ \mathrm{mV}\)). What is \(v_o\), in V?
questions.explanation:
Superpose: the signal gives \(-50\times10\ \mathrm{mV}=-0.5\ \mathrm{V}\); the offset gives \(+(1+50)\times1\ \mathrm{mV}=+0.051\ \mathrm{V}\).
\(v_o=-0.5+0.051=-0.449\ \mathrm{V}\). A 10% error from a 1 mV offset! Common mistake: amplifying \(V_{os}\) by 50 (giving \(-0.45\ \mathrm{V}\)).

questions.prompt: In a non-inverting amplifier (gain \(1+R_2/R_1=100\)), a large capacitor is placed in series with \(R_1\) (between \(R_1\) and ground). What happens to the output offset due to \(V_{os}\)?
options: It is unchanged at \(100\,V_{os}\)
It drops to just \(V_{os}\): at DC the capacitor is open so the DC gain is 1, while signals well above the RC corner still get gain 100
It becomes zero
It increases to \(\infty\) since the DC gain becomes infinite
questions.explanation: At DC no current flows through \(R_1\), so the feedback network becomes a direct connection: the circuit is a follower for DC and \(V_o=V_{os}\). At signal frequencies the capacitor is a short and the gain is \(1+R_2/R_1\). This 'AC-coupled feedback' trick is common in audio amplifiers.

questions.prompt: Preview of datasheets. A thermocouple produces \(40\ \mu\mathrm{V/^\circ C}\). Its amplifier's op-amp has \(V_{os}=0.5\ \mathrm{mV}\). How large a temperature error (in °C) does the untrimmed offset look like?
questions.explanation: The offset adds to the input like a signal: \(\dfrac{0.5\ \mathrm{mV}}{40\ \mu\mathrm{V/^\circ C}}=12.5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\). Precision sensor front-ends need low-offset or 'zero-drift' op-amps, which is why you read that line of a datasheet first.

questions.prompt: Preview of input bias current. Another DC error appears as an extra \(0.3\ \mathrm{mV}\) at the \(+\) input (bias current flowing through the source resistance). Worst case it has the same sign as \(V_{os}=1\ \mathrm{mV}\). In a gain-20 non-inverting amplifier, what is the worst-case output DC error, in mV?
questions.explanation: Both are DC sources at the same input, so they add before the gain: \((1+0.3)\ \mathrm{mV}\times20=26\ \mathrm{mV}\). The bias-current skill shows where such input voltages come from and how to cancel them.

questions.prompt: Preview of datasheets. An op-amp's offset is trimmed to zero at 25 °C. The datasheet lists an offset drift of \(10\ \mu\mathrm{V/^\circ C}\). The circuit (gain 100) then runs at 75 °C. What output offset do you expect?
options: About 50 mV: \(10\ \mu\mathrm{V/^\circ C}\times50\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}=0.5\ \mathrm{mV}\) at the input, times 100
0 V, since it was trimmed
About 5 mV
About 0.5 mV
questions.explanation:
Trimming (reader Sec. 18.2.2) zeroes the offset at ONE temperature. Drift is a separate spec: \(\Delta V_{os}=10\ \mu\mathrm{V/^\circ C}\times50=0.5\ \mathrm{mV}\), and the output sees \(100\times0.5\ \mathrm{mV}=50\ \mathrm{mV}\).
• 0.5 mV forgets the gain; 5 mV is a factor-of-10 slip.
